narrations.title: Timeline — 80 Years of Canadian Government Actions
narrations.narration: The 1940s. Post-War Reconstruction. Canada emerges from World War II. The Veterans Charter promises housing, education, and support for returning soldiers. The foundation is laid for the social contract that the government will later break.

narrations.title: Timeline — 80 Years of Canadian Government Actions
narrations.narration: The 1950s. Cold War and Broken Promises. Canada enters the Korean War, losing 516 soldiers. NORAD is established. The Avro Arrow, Canada's most advanced fighter jet, is built then destroyed along with 14,000 jobs — permanently crippling Canadian aerospace.

narrations.title: Timeline — 80 Years of Canadian Government Actions
narrations.narration: The 1960s. Rights and Revolution. Indigenous Canadians finally gain the right to vote federally. The Quiet Revolution transforms Quebec. Residential schools continue operating. The seeds of modern Canadian civil rights are planted amid ongoing systemic failures.

narrations.title: Timeline — 80 Years of Canadian Government Actions
narrations.narration: The 1970s. Crisis and Multiculturalism. Pierre Trudeau invokes the War Measures Act during the October Crisis — the only peacetime use in Canadian history. Nearly 500 people arrested without charge. Canada adopts official multiculturalism policy. The Parti Quebecois wins Quebec on a sovereignty platform.

narrations.title: Timeline — 80 Years of Canadian Government Actions
narrations.narration: The 1980s. Constitution and Free Trade. The National Energy Program devastates Alberta. The Charter of Rights and Freedoms is patriated in 1982 without Quebec's consent. Mulroney signs the Free Trade Agreement with the US and the failed Meech Lake Accord.

narrations.title: Timeline — 80 Years of Canadian Government Actions
narrations.narration: The 1990s. Scandals and Near-Secession. The Charlottetown Accord fails. The 1995 Quebec referendum comes within 54,000 votes of breaking apart Canada. The Somalia Affair exposes Canadian soldiers torturing and killing a Somali teenager. The Sponsorship Scandal begins.

narrations.title: Timeline — 80 Years of Canadian Government Actions
narrations.narration: The 2000s. War, Scandal and Reckoning. Canada deploys to Afghanistan — 158 soldiers killed, over 2,000 wounded. The Sponsorship Scandal brings down the Liberal government. The Gomery Commission reveals systematic corruption. Stephen Harper wins on an accountability platform.

narrations.title: Timeline — 80 Years of Canadian Government Actions
narrations.narration: The 2010s. Pipeline Politics and MAID. Afghanistan combat mission ends. Pipeline battles rage between provinces and the federal government. MAID is legalized in 2016 with Bill C-14, then expanded with Bill C-7. The foreign interference crisis begins to surface through CSIS intelligence leaks.

narrations.title: Timeline — 80 Years of Canadian Government Actions
narrations.narration: The 2020s. Emergencies, Debt and Collapse. COVID lockdowns and 89.9 billion in pandemic spending. The Emergencies Act is invoked against the Freedom Convoy. Bank accounts are frozen. MAID deaths accelerate past 15,000 per year. The national debt doubles. Foreign interference is confirmed across multiple elections.

narrations.title: How Canada Treats Its Veterans — The Data
narrations.narration: How Canada Treats Its Veterans — The Data. Higher suicide rates. Months-long waits for disability benefits. And when they ask for a wheelchair ramp, they're offered death. Every number below comes from the Government of Canada's own reports.

narrations.title: How Canada Treats Its Veterans — The Data
narrations.narration: Veteran suicide. Male veterans die by suicide at 1.4 times the civilian rate. Female veterans at 1.9 times. This elevated risk has persisted for forty-two years. The government has known.

narrations.title: How Canada Treats Its Veterans — The Data
narrations.narration: The disability benefits backlog. Only forty-seven percent of applications now meet the sixteen-week standard. The backlog doubled from five thousand six hundred to over eleven thousand in a single year.

narrations.title: How Canada Treats Its Veterans — The Data
narrations.narration: Mental health claim denials. Of fifteen thousand veterans who applied for mental health disability benefits, twenty-four percent were denied. Nearly one in four told their suffering does not qualify.

narrations.title: How Canada Treats Its Veterans — The Data
narrations.narration: MAID — offered death instead of help. A Paralympian veteran asked for a wheelchair ramp. The government's response: we can help you die. At least four to five confirmed cases of veterans being offered MAID by a Veterans Affairs employee.

narrations.title: How Canada Treats Its Veterans — The Data
narrations.narration: The math. A MAID procedure costs twenty-five hundred dollars. A wheelchair ramp costs three to eight thousand. Annual disability benefits cost fifteen to forty thousand per veteran. It is cheaper to kill a veteran than to provide a ramp for two years.

narrations.title: How Canada Treats Its Veterans — The Data
narrations.narration: My case. A veteran reported foreign interference targeting the mental health infrastructure that serves soldiers. The response was not investigation. It was prosecution. The message: stay silent or be destroyed.

narrations.title: How Canada Treats Its Veterans — The Data
narrations.narration: Veteran homelessness. Three to five thousand Canadian veterans are homeless on any given night. Veterans are overrepresented in shelter populations by two to four times their proportion of the general population.

narrations.title: How Canada Treats Its Veterans — The Data
narrations.narration: The veteran-to-MAID pipeline. Inadequate transition, denied claims, impossible wait times, and then an offer of death. The government's own data documents every link in this chain. This is not random failure. It is a connected pipeline.

narrations.narration: Lest We Forget. How Canada Betrayed Its Veterans. They were promised a country worthy of their sacrifice. They were given a backlog, a budget cut, and a brochure for medical assistance in dying.

narrations.title: Lest We Forget — How Canada Betrayed Its Veterans
narrations.narration: Section 1. Veterans Affairs By the Numbers. A department failing the people it exists to serve. Over 11,000 veterans wait in the disability claims backlog while the department inexplicably lapses hundreds of millions in unspent funding.

narrations.title: Lest We Forget — How Canada Betrayed Its Veterans
narrations.narration: Section 2. The Medical Assistance in Dying Question. Veterans who called seeking assistance for injuries sustained in service were systematically offered state-sponsored euthanasia. No veteran should ever be offered death when they are asking for help to live.

narrations.title: Lest We Forget — How Canada Betrayed Its Veterans
narrations.narration: Section 3. The Funding Gap. Between 2018 and 2023, the government lapsed over 3 billion dollars in approved veterans funding. Money was budgeted, but Veterans Affairs simply failed to spend it on the people it was meant for.

narrations.title: Lest We Forget — How Canada Betrayed Its Veterans
narrations.narration: Section 4. Phoenix Pay and Veterans. Broken Twice. The 2.2 billion dollar Phoenix Pay failure devastated veterans transitioning to federal employment, leaving many without paychecks while simultaneously navigating the disability backlog.

narrations.title: Lest We Forget — How Canada Betrayed Its Veterans
narrations.narration: Section 5. The Office Closures. In 2014, the Harper government closed 9 Veterans Affairs district offices across Canada. Veterans in rural and remote communities lost face-to-face access to caseworkers. Some had to travel hundreds of kilometres for appointments. Many simply stopped seeking help.

narrations.title: Lest We Forget — How Canada Betrayed Its Veterans
narrations.narration: Section 6. Operational Stress Injuries. The invisible wounds. Post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, anxiety, and moral injury affect tens of thousands of Canadian veterans. Wait times for mental health services at Veterans Affairs routinely exceed 6 months. The veteran suicide rate remains significantly higher than the general population.

narrations.title: Lest We Forget — How Canada Betrayed Its Veterans
narrations.narration: Section 7. The Record of Broken Promises. Decade after decade, Canadian governments have promised veterans better care, faster processing, more support. And decade after decade, those promises have been broken. The Veterans Charter was supposed to fix everything. It didn't. The New Veterans Charter was supposed to modernize everything. It created new problems.

narrations.title: Lest We Forget — How Canada Betrayed Its Veterans

Canada broke that promise.

narrations.title: Whistleblower Failures

narrations.title: Whistleblower Failures

An independent protection agency outside political control. Reverse burden of proof — employers must prove reprisal was not a factor. Criminal penalties for retaliation. These are not radical proposals. They exist in every allied nation except Canada.

narrations.title: Whistleblower Failures
narrations.narration: The Criminal Code irony. Canada's Criminal Code contains no specific offence for retaliating against a whistleblower. A government employee who exposes billions in fraud has no legal shield. The person who fires them faces no criminal consequence. The law protects the institution, not the individual who tries to fix it.

narrations.title: RCMP Reform

narrations.title: RCMP Reform

Officers are leaving for municipal forces. Rural communities dependent on RCMP policing face growing response time gaps.

narrations.title: RCMP Reform

Binding oversight with enforcement power. Mandatory body cameras. A civilian intelligence review board. Real whistleblower protection. Every commission has recommended these changes. None have been implemented.

narrations.title: RCMP Reform

The institution cannot reform itself. External, binding, enforceable oversight is the only path forward.
